fetched_contents.text: Effect of timing of artificial insemination in relation to onset of standing estrus on pregnancy per AI in Nili-Ravi buffalo Abstract The aim of the present study was to determine the optimum time of artificial insemination after the beginning of standing estrus in buffalo. Nili-Ravi buffalo (n = 109) during breeding season were exposed to teaser bull at 12 hours interval to determine the standing heat (0 h). Buffalo were randomly allocated to different time groups and a single artificial insemination was performed either at 0 h (n = 30), 12 h (n = 27), 24 h (n = 28) or 36 h (n = 24). In a subset of buffalo (n = 38) ultrasonography was performed, twice daily from 0 h (onset of standing heat) to determine the time of ovulation. Pregnancy diagnosis was performed 35-40 days after AI. Results revealed that mean time of ovulation from onset of standing heat was 34.7 ± 0.96 h (range 30 to 42 h). Higher (P < 0.05) pregnancy per AI were achieved in buffalo when inseminated at 24 h (15/28; 53%) compared to 0 h (8/30; 26%) and 36 h (3/24; 13%). Pregnancy per AI, was in-between, in buffalo, inseminated at 12 h (10/27; 37%) and did not differ (P > 0.05) with those bred either at 24 h or 0 h. The odds ratio further confirmed that the occurrence of pregnancy per AI was two times higher in buffalo inseminated at 24 h as compared to those at 12 h. It is concluded that optimal pregnancy per AI can be achieved when buffalo are bred artificially 24 h after the onset of standing heat. Keywords: Nili-Ravi buffalo, timing of insemination, standing heat, pregnancy per AI Introduction Artificial insemination (AI) has played a major role in genetic selection, disease control and cost effectiveness of breeding in dairy cattle ( Vishwanath, 2003 ; López-Gatius, 2012 ). Although, considerable research and development has taken place in estrus and ovulation synchronization in cows and buffalo with use of fixed time AI (Warriach et al ., 2007; Rossi et al., 2014 ; Yousuf et al., 2015 ), yet its application in vast majority of buffalo population of Asia is negligible. In contrast, traditional use of AI at detected estrus is much higher, however, fertility is generally compromised. Several factors which can affect fertility include heat stress ( Shenhe et al., 2018 ) semen quality, estrus signs, technician and timing of insemination in buffalo ( Anzar et al., 2003 ). When AI was introduced in cattle in 1930’s ( Foote, 2002 ), the proper time of insemination became the most logical question. Series of classical experiments on ovulation and insemination timings addressed this issue in dairy cattle. Minimum number of cows returned to estrus when bred artificially 12 hours after the beginning of standing estrus ( Trimberger, 1948 ) that laid the foundation for AM-PM rule, i.e., a cow detected in standing heat in the morning should be bred artificially in the evening and vice versa. This method ensures sufficient time for sperm to capacitate and reach the proper site of fertilization in the oviduct ( Yanagimachi, 1981 ; Bedford, 1983 ). Owing to the anatomical and physiological similarities, a natural consequence was the adoption of AI methods in water buffalo from cattle protocols. Consequently, without gaining basic knowledge of timing of ovulation, AM-PM rule was adopted in the buffalo ( Drost, 2007 ). This practice resulted in reduced number of pregnancies leading to less adaptability of AI by the farmer community ( Anzar et al., 2003 ). Paradoxically, whether or not, this AM-PM rule holds true in water buffalo has not yet been systemically investigated. Suboptimal pregnancy rates after AI could be a reason that genetic selection in buffalo did not take place at the same pace as in cows. AI must take place at a precise interval from ovulation thus ensuring successful fertilization. In case of early AI, the sperm would lose fertilizing ability ( Hawk, 1987 ) while in case of late AI, the ova would become aged which may cause failure of fertilization ( Hunter and Greve, 1997 ). With the expansion of AI programs in buffalo it was envisioned that the technique used in cattle required modifications in order to achieve the best results in buffalo ( Cockrill, 1974 ). Pioneer work in buffalo, based on rectal palpation, revealed that ovulation occurred at 34 h after the beginning of estrus ( Kanai and Shimizu, 1983 ), in contrast to 24 h in dairy cows after onset of standing heat ( Rajamahendran et al., 1989 ). Using ultrasonography, we reported that time of ovulation in buffalo was 31 h after the onset of standing heat ( Warriach et al., 2008 ). Higher conceptions were reported when AI was performed at later stage of estrus in buffalo under field conditions but without precise confirmation of ovulation ( Srivastava et al., 1998 ). The reported delayed time of ovulation and lowered fertility in buffalo compared with dairy cows prompted us to hypothesize that a time interval of 24 h between onset of standing estrus and AI will be optimal to improve fertility in buffalo. There is no systematic study available which have shown the relationship of varying time of insemination with fertility. The objective of the present study was to determine the effect of insemination timing on pregnancy per AI in buffalo. The experimental design also allowed us to examine the optimal time interval between AI and ovulation time. fetched_contents.text: Ovarian follicular dynamics during the estrous cycle in buffalo (Bubalus bubalis) The growth, selection, regression and ovulation of ovarian follicles was ultrasonically monitored in 30 Murrah buffalo throughout a spontaneous estrous cycle during the breeding season (autumn). Examinations revealed that follicular growth during the estrous cycle occurs in waves; the buffalo showed 1-wave (3.3%, n = 1), 2-wave (63.3%, n = 19) or 3-wave (33.3%, n = 10) follicular growth. Nonetheless, buffaloes exhibit unique reproductive behavior, which complicates the insemination process. These animals demonstrate inconsistent periods (ranging from 6–48 h) of mounting acceptance. Therefore, timed artificial insemination (TAI) has surfaced as a useful technique for advancing buffalo breeding initiatives and omits the need for heat detection. Estrus signs in buffaloes can be used to time insemination, but their reliability varies and they change over the estrous cycle. The most reliable behavioral sign is “standing to be ridden” or “standing for mounting,” which is described as the best reliable sign of estrus in buffaloes [N1-R3], and teaser buffalo bulls can detect buffaloes in estrus by observing this sign [N6-R3]. This sign is also emphasized as a key detection issue and one of the main factors affecting fertility status [N6-R4]. 

Other common behavioral signs include restlessness, aggression, bellowing, tail rising, homosexual mounting, abnormal posture, and pelvic movements [N1-R2]. These are useful but less specific than standing heat. Mucus discharge and swollen vulva are also noted as salient estrus signs, though their expression is weak and varies seasonally [N1-F1]. The same source highlights that buffalo are “much known as 'Peculiar Shy Breeder'” and that estrus signs can be difficult to detect because acceptance of the male is considered the most reliable indicator [N1-F1]. 

The timing of signs changes over the estrous cycle. Buffalo estrus is often described as lasting 6–30 hours, with key signs such as restlessness, riding herd mates, vaginal mucus discharge, and swollen vulva [N1-R5]. In the context of artificial insemination, standing heat is treated as the primary sign and the basis for insemination timing, because ovulation occurs 25–30 hours after the onset of standing activity [N2-R2]. Another source reports that the optimal time to inseminate is mid to late estrus, ideally around 12 hours after the first signs of standing heat [N2-R3], while a more specific buffalo study concludes that optimal pregnancy per AI occurs when buffalo are bred 24 hours after the onset of standing heat [N2-F2]. This suggests that the timing of insemination should not be taken at the first sign, but should follow a window that accounts for the lag between behavioral onset and ovulation.

Behavioral vs biological signs provide different timing cues. Behavioral signs are the main practical cues used by farmers, especially standing heat and related restlessness or mounting behavior [N1-F1][N1-R2][N6-R3]. Biological signs, such as mucus discharge, are also used but are described as weak and variable [N1-F1][N1-R4]. In practice, biological signs may help confirm estrus, but they are less reliable for timing decisions than the behavioral sign of standing heat [N1-R4][N1-F1]. The literature also indicates that buffalo may exhibit silent estrus, which complicates biological confirmation and requires more precise detection methods [N4-F4].

Overall, the evidence supports using standing heat as the most reliable timing cue, with insemination ideally occurring after standing heat has been observed and within a narrow ovulation window, such as 12–24 hours after onset [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-F2]. Behavioral signs are easier to observe and more consistent for practical decision-making, while biological signs can supplement detection but are less reliable and more variable [N1-F1][N1-R4].

A buffalo study found that estrous cycles can have 1, 2, or 3 follicular waves, with 2-wave cycles being the most common [N3-F3]. This follicular-wave structure is important because it means that the timing of follicular growth, selection, regression, and ovulation is not strictly uniform across all buffalo [N3-F3].

The evidence also emphasizes that the number of waves is associated with luteal phase length and cycle length [N3-F3]. This matters because longer luteal phases and different follicular patterns may alter the window in which insemination should occur and influence conception rates. These differences mean that buffalo require more precise timing than cattle and that blanket cattle-based rules may be suboptimal [N2-F2][N3-F3].

In summary, buffalo physiology constrains optimal timing because cycle length, ovulation timing, follicular waves, and corpus luteum status vary, while enabling more precise synchronization and timing when these factors are understood [N3-R3][N3-F3][N2-F2]. ## How to optimize insemination timing in buffaloes using estrus signs to improve fertility

Optimizing insemination timing in buffaloes requires using estrus signs to identify the best moment to inseminate, while recognizing that buffalo physiology and management constraints make timing more complex than in some cattle systems. The evidence suggests that the most reliable practical cue is standing heat, but buffalo also exhibit a range of behavioral and biological signs, and their estrous cycle is variable. At the same time, estrus detection is often unreliable enough to justify synchronization and fixed-time insemination as important tools. The best approach is therefore a combination of careful sign-based timing, synchronization, and broader reproductive management.

---

## 1) Use the most reliable estrus signs to identify the timing window

Buffaloes rely on both behavioral and biological signs to detect estrus, but the most reliable sign is **“standing to be ridden”** or **standing for mounting** [N1-R3]. This is also described as the best reliable sign of estrus in buffaloes [N6-R3]. Farmers and observers should prioritize this sign because it is easier to recognize and has stronger predictive value than many other behavioral signs.

Other common behavioral signs include **restlessness, aggression, bellowing, tail rising, homosexual mounting, abnormal posture, and pelvic movements** [N1-R2]. These are useful but less specific than standing heat. The literature also notes that **mucus discharge and swollen vulva** are salient signs, though their expression is weak and varies seasonally [N1-F1][N1-R4]. In other words, behavioral signs are usually more practical and more consistent, while biological signs can supplement detection but are less reliable and more variable [N1-F1][N1-R4].

### How the timing of signs changes over the estrous cycle

Buffalo estrus is often described as lasting 6–30 hours, with key signs such as restlessness, riding herd mates, vaginal mucus discharge, and swollen vulva [N1-R5]. In the context of artificial insemination, **standing heat is the primary sign and determines the time of insemination** because ovulation occurs 25–30 hours after the onset of standing activity [N2-R2]. Another source says the optimal time to inseminate is **mid to late estrus, ideally around 12 hours after the first signs of standing heat** [N2-R3]. A more specific buffalo study concludes that **optimal pregnancy per AI occurs when buffalo are bred 24 hours after the onset of standing heat** [N2-F2].

This means the timing cue should not be taken at the first sign, but should follow a window that accounts for the lag between behavioral onset and ovulation. The evidence supports a practical interpretation: observe standing heat, then inseminate **within 12–24 hours after onset**, with 24 hours being the most supported buffalo-specific window [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-F2].

### Behavioral vs biological signs provide different timing cues

Behavioral signs are the main practical cues used by farmers, especially **standing heat** and related restlessness or mounting behavior [N1-F1][N1-R2][N6-R3]. Biological signs, such as mucus discharge, are also used but are described as weak and variable [N1-F1][N1-R4]. In practice, biological signs may help confirm estrus, but they are less reliable for timing decisions than the behavioral sign of standing heat [N1-R4][N1-F1]. The literature also indicates that buffalo may exhibit **silent estrus**, which complicates biological confirmation and requires more precise detection methods [N4-F4].

So the best practical strategy is to combine **standing heat as the primary timing cue** with supplementary biological signs when available, while recognizing that biological signs are not as reliable or consistent as behavior [N1-R4][N1-F1].

This is a crucial distinction because it shows why buffalo timing should be treated as a separate problem.

---

## 3) Practical strategies to improve fertility through better timing

Practical strategies to improve fertility through better timing include **reducing missed cycles**, **using synchronization programs to refine estrus detection**, and addressing factors beyond timing that influence insemination success.

### Reduce missed cycles through better management

Breeding management practices that reduce missed cycles include keeping proper fertility records, encouraging farmers to monitor individual animals, and using better heat-detection methods [N5-R4]. A review emphasizes that efficient reproductive management in water buffaloes relies on understanding biology and using **fixed-time artificial insemination (FTAI)** [N5-R3]. Another source states that farmers should be encouraged to keep proper fertility records of individual cows in their herds for efficient reproductive management [N5-R4]. These practices help reduce missed cycles by improving detection and recordkeeping rather than relying solely on sporadic observation [N5-R4][N5-R3].

### Use synchronization programs to refine estrus detection

Synchronization programs are especially relevant because buffaloes often exhibit **poor overt estrus expression** and seasonality, making heat detection difficult [N4-R5][N4-F4]. The evidence states that **estrus synchronization and timed inseminations can overcome these two problems** [N4-R5], and that **fixed-time artificial insemination (TAI)** enhances reproductive management and genetic progress by synchronizing estrus and optimizing insemination timing [N4-R2][N4-F4]. 

Because buffalo may have **inconsistent periods of mounting acceptance**, timed artificial insemination (TAI) has emerged as a useful technique that **omits the need for heat detection** [N4-F4]. The review also notes that **TAI enhances reproductive management and genetic progress by synchronizing estrus and optimizing insemination timing** [N4-R2]. This indicates that synchronization can improve fertility even when heat detection is unreliable [N4-R3][N4-F4].

### Address factors beyond timing that influence insemination success

Factors besides timing that influence insemination success include **breeding season, hormonal treatments, environmental conditions, uterine infections, reproductive tract abnormalities, hormonal dysfunction, and semen quality** [N4-F4][N5-R5]. The buffalo review emphasizes that buffalo reproductive efficiency is influenced by **heat detection, environmental conditions, hormonal treatments, and seasonality of breeding** [N4-F4]. Another source states that **repeat breeding is multifactorial** and can result from **uterine infections, reproductive tract abnormalities, hormonal dysfunction, and other factors** [N5-R5]. 

This means that even with good timing, insemination success depends on a broader reproductive environment [N4-F4][N5-R5]. So timing alone is not enough; fertility improvement also requires attention to **health, seasonality, hormonal status, and semen quality**.

---

## 4) Limitations and uncertainty in using estrus signs for timing decisions

The use of estrus signs for timing decisions is limited by **unreliability, variability, and the difficulty of distinguishing true from false signs**. Buffalo heat detection is described as one of the main factors affecting fertility status and as a key issue that should be prioritized [N6-R4]. The same source notes that **inefficient heat detection reduces the fertility status of the herd** [N6-R4]. This indicates that unreliable signs can **delay or mislead insemination decisions** because farmers may inseminate too early, too late, or not at all [N6-R4].

Behavioral signs are not always reliable. While **standing to be ridden** is the best reliable sign of estrus, the literature notes **wide variability in estrus detection** and that buffalo may exhibit **silent estrus** [N1-F1][N6-R3]. Another source explicitly says that estrus detection is the most important factor for dairy animals to get them pregnant on time for efficient production [N6-R5]. This highlights the risk that poor heat detection can lead to **missed cycles** and **repeat breeding**.

Poor heat detection affects conception rates and repeat breeding. The buffalo review states that **artificial insemination programs are highly influenced by heat detection** [N4-F4]. Another source states that **repeat breeding is multifactorial** and can result from **uterine infections, reproductive tract abnormalities, hormonal dysfunction, and other factors** [N5-R5]. This suggests that even when timing is correct, poor heat detection can indirectly contribute to repeat breeding by causing missed inseminations [N4-F4][N5-R5].

Synchronization is needed to compensate for sign limitations. Because buffalo may have **inconsistent periods of mounting acceptance** and exhibit **poor overt estrus expression**, **timed artificial insemination (TAI)** has emerged as a useful technique that **omits the need for heat detection** [N4-F4]. The evidence states that **estrus synchronization and timed inseminations can overcome the problems of poor overt estrus expression and seasonality** [N4-R5]. **Fixed-time AI** is described as a way to advance buffalo breeding initiatives and improve reproductive management [N4-R2]. This indicates that synchronization is especially valuable when heat detection is unreliable or inconsistent [N4-R5][N4-F4].

---

## 5) Integrated recommendation for optimizing insemination timing

Based on the evidence, the best integrated strategy for optimizing insemination timing in buffaloes is:

1. **Use standing heat as the primary timing cue**, because it is the most reliable practical sign [N1-R3][N6-R3].
2. **Inseminate within a window of 12–24 hours after the onset of standing heat**, with 24 hours being the most supported buffalo-specific window [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-F2].
3. **Use supplementary biological signs** such as mucus discharge and swollen vulva, but recognize that they are less reliable and more variable than behavior [N1-F1][N1-R4].
4. **Account for buffalo physiology**: buffalo have a variable estrous cycle, delayed ovulation relative to standing heat, and more follicular waves than cattle [N3-R3][N2-F2][N3-F3].
5. **Reduce missed cycles** through better recordkeeping, individual monitoring, and improved heat detection [N5-R4][N5-R3].
6. **Use synchronization programs** when heat detection is unreliable, because estrus synchronization and timed inseminations can overcome poor overt estrus expression and seasonality [N4-R5][N4-F4].
7. **Address factors beyond timing** such as breeding season, hormonal treatments, environmental conditions, and semen quality, because those also strongly affect fertility [N4-F4][N5-R5].

---

## Bottom line

The evidence supports a nuanced approach: buffalo timing should be based on **standing heat as the main cue**, with a practical insemination window of **12–24 hours after onset** [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-F2]. However, buffalo physiology makes timing more complex than cattle, because ovulation is later and cycles are more variable [N2-F2][N3-F3]. Poor heat detection is a major limitation, so synchronization and fixed-time insemination should be used when detection is unreliable [N4-R5][N4-F4]. The best fertility outcome comes from combining careful sign-based timing, synchronization, and broader reproductive management [N7][N8][N9][N10].

The most reliable behavioral sign is “standing to be ridden” or “standing for mounting,” which is described as the best reliable sign of estrus in buffaloes [N1-R3], and teaser buffalo bulls can detect buffaloes in estrus by observing this sign [N6-R3]. This sign is also emphasized as a key detection issue and one of the main factors affecting fertility status [N6-R4]. 

Other common behavioral signs include restlessness, aggression, bellowing, tail rising, homosexual mounting, abnormal posture, and pelvic movements [N1-R2]. These are useful but less specific than standing heat. Mucus discharge and swollen vulva are also noted as salient estrus signs, though their expression is weak and varies seasonally [N1-F1]. The same source highlights that buffalo are “much known as 'Peculiar Shy Breeder'” and that estrus signs can be difficult to detect because acceptance of the male is considered the most reliable indicator [N1-F1]. 

The timing of signs changes over the estrous cycle. Buffalo estrus is often described as lasting 6–30 hours, with key signs such as restlessness, riding herd mates, vaginal mucus discharge, and swollen vulva [N1-R5]. In the context of artificial insemination, standing heat is treated as the primary sign and the basis for insemination timing, because ovulation occurs 25–30 hours after the onset of standing activity [N2-R2]. Another source reports that the optimal time to inseminate is mid to late estrus, ideally around 12 hours after the first signs of standing heat [N2-R3], while a more specific buffalo study concludes that optimal pregnancy per AI occurs when buffalo are bred 24 hours after the onset of standing heat [N2-F2]. This suggests that the timing of insemination should not be taken at the first sign, but should follow a window that accounts for the lag between behavioral onset and ovulation.

Behavioral vs biological signs provide different timing cues. Behavioral signs are the main practical cues used by farmers, especially standing heat and related restlessness or mounting behavior [N1-F1][N1-R2][N6-R3]. Biological signs, such as mucus discharge, are also used but are described as weak and variable [N1-F1][N1-R4]. In practice, biological signs may help confirm estrus, but they are less reliable for timing decisions than the behavioral sign of standing heat [N1-R4][N1-F1]. The literature also indicates that buffalo may exhibit silent estrus, which complicates biological confirmation and requires more precise detection methods [N4-F4].

Overall, the evidence supports using standing heat as the most reliable timing cue, with insemination ideally occurring after standing heat has been observed and within a narrow ovulation window, such as 12–24 hours after onset [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-F2]. Behavioral signs are easier to observe and more consistent for practical decision-making, while biological signs can supplement detection but are less reliable and more variable [N1-F1][N1-R4].

The evidence also emphasizes that the number of waves is associated with luteal phase length and cycle length [N3-F3].
